items.title: The Wahine storm
items.summary: On 10 April 1968 (NZST), ex-tropical Cyclone Giselle and a low from the south combined into a severe storm over central New Zealand. Renewed development outside the tropics brought prolonged southerlies across Wellington and Cook Strait. Measured gusts reached 198 km/h at Kelburn and 187 km/h at Wellington Airport. Buildings and power lines were damaged, and the ferry Wahine struck Barrett Reef and later capsized in Wellington Harbour; NZHistory counts 53 deaths from the wreck, including two later deaths.

impacts.text: NZHistory attributes 53 deaths to the Wahine wreck in New Zealand: 51 people died on the day, one several weeks later, and another in 1990 from injuries sustained in the disaster. Most deaths occurred on the Eastbourne side of Wellington Harbour, where survivors were swept towards rocks and surf.

NIWA records three other deaths in Wellington caused by the high winds. Roofs were lifted, windows smashed and trees blown onto houses. Fallen trees and power and trolley bus lines, together with flooding, disrupted road and rail travel.
NIWA reports NZ$194 million in insurance payouts for the storm, in 2008 prices.

history.text: MetService forecaster Erick Brenstrum’s later account says the Wahine was warned of possible southerlies above 110 km/h in Cook Strait as the low crossed the North Island.

A later MetService review describes forecasts improving with satellites, radar, automatic weather stations and better computer models. These were broad changes over the following decades; the review does not identify a reform caused by the wreck.

why_interesting.text: Giselle had lost its tropical cyclone structure before reaching northern New Zealand. An intense trough high in the atmosphere then helped it strengthen again. The damaging system drew on contrasts between warm and cold air as it became a storm outside the tropics.

The low moved rapidly from east of Northland across Tauranga towards Castlepoint. By about 9 a.m. NZST on 10 April it was east of Cape Palliser, while Wellington experienced some of its strongest winds.

The city stations establish the scale of the wind: Kelburn measured a gust of 107 knots (198 km/h) on 10 April, and Wellington Airport reached 101 knots (187 km/h), around 9 a.m. NZST at the airport. Both came from the south-southwest. These are gusts, rather than sustained wind speeds.

Higher gusts were reported on exposed coasts: a provisional Meteorological Service list gives Oteranga Bay 145 knots, while a later table gives 131 knots; these conflicting figures do not establish a secure single maximum for the storm.

The dangerous seas grew in the southern approaches to Cook Strait. Strong winds and falling pressure also raised the water level in Wellington Harbour. NIWA stresses that the storm waves were reconstructed afterwards, rather than measured at the time.

Cook Strait and the surrounding hills modify the regional wind, making exposure important even within Wellington. The contrast between nearby stations is difficult to reproduce on ERA5’s roughly 31 km grid.

items.reanalysis: ERA5 places the lowest centre at 967 hPa off the Wairarapa coast at 21 UTC 9 Apr, compared with a published ship reading of 963 hPa whose exact time and position are not given. Its largest hourly gusts at Kelburn and Wellington Airport are both about 44 m/s in the hour ending 23 UTC 9 Apr, below the measured 55 and 52 m/s respectively, and later than the airport peak around 9 a.m. NZST. Oteranga Bay reaches about 43 m/s in that same hour, but the conflicting published gusts there prevent a precise judgement of the shortfall. Sparse observations in 1968 and the smoothed hills and coasts in ERA5 make local peaks and their timing uncertain.

items.title: The Great Storm of October 1987
items.summary: A deep Atlantic depression crossed southern England during the night of 15–16 October 1987, bringing destructive winds to England and northern France. The Met Office counts 18 deaths directly caused by the storm in England. About 15 million trees were blown down, and at the peak 3 million homes and businesses were without electricity. Gusts reached 98 knots at Shoreham-by-Sea and at least 216 km/h on the Normandy coast.

impacts.text: The Met Office counts 18 direct storm deaths in England. This excludes deaths in other countries.

The Forestry Commission estimated 15 million fallen trees, representing 3.9 million cubic metres of timber. It reported 3 million householders and businesses without electricity at the peak of the cuts, and no Southern Region trains running on the morning of 16 October.
Buildings and boats were damaged. Fallen trees blocked transport and broke power lines. Gatwick Airport closed.

history.text: Later forecasts shifted the main threat south. Evening broadcasts emphasised rain and missed the exceptional winds. Michael Fish denied that a hurricane was coming; the Met Office says he meant another Atlantic system.
Emergency authorities received warnings, and the Ministry of Defence was alerted at 0135 UTC on 16 October.

Afterwards, more ocean buoys were deployed to watch the seas south-west of the British Isles, and the Met Office set up the National Severe Weather Warning Service to warn emergency services and the public.

why_interesting.text: The low deepened by 17 hPa in 12 hours as it crossed the Bay of Biscay. The pressure rises behind it were exceptional: 12 hPa in one hour at Hurn, near Bournemouth.
Its track took it from west of Spain to north-west of Brittany by 00 GMT 16 Oct, over Exeter at 02 GMT and to Hull around 05–06 GMT. The most damaging winds lay south and south-east of the track.
It became a key case for the sting jet: air descending from the cloud head near its hooked tip, bringing the damaging winds seen in the dry slot.
Some records were revised. The Met Office later reduced Gorleston's 106 knots to 85 knots because the anemometer cups were bent, leaving Shoreham as the strongest measured gust in England.

items.reanalysis: ERA5 reaches 951 hPa off Brittany at 22 UTC 15 Oct, close to published central-pressure analyses of 952–953 hPa around 00 GMT 16 Oct. Its peak gusts at Shoreham are 40 m/s during 03–04 UTC 16 Oct and at Pointe du Roc 35 m/s during 00–01 UTC 16 Oct, below the station evidence. The largest shortfall is at Pointe du Roc, where the recorder reached 60 m/s, so the actual peak remains uncertain. These differences likely reflect the coarse representation of coastlines, exposed headlands and small wind features; London’s rooftop instrument also differs from a standard surface wind measurement.

items.title: Storms Lothar and Martin
items.summary: Lothar crossed northern France, southern Germany and Switzerland on 26 December 1999. Martin followed across western and southern France on 27 December and into the next morning. Rapid deepening in a powerful Atlantic westerly flow brought measured gusts of 173 km/h at Paris-Orly during Lothar and 198 km/h at Chassiron during Martin. The French government review counted 92 deaths in France, with widespread damage to forests, buildings and power lines; SDES lists total French damage of €15 billion in 1999 prices.

impacts.text: The French government's July 2000 review counted 92 deaths in France, including accidents during rescue and early repairs as well as the storms themselves. It noted further deaths during subsequent recovery work, so this is not a final count of all later consequences.

Trees were uprooted, roofs damaged and electricity and telephone networks broken. Forests suffered extensive losses, notably in Lorraine, while fallen trees and damaged infrastructure disrupted roads and railways.
SDES, drawing on the ONRN disaster database, lists €15 billion in total damage in France, in 1999 prices. This includes insured and uninsured damage.

history.text: The government review found that regional bulletins before Lothar underestimated the wind strength. Stronger warnings followed when the storm was already reaching France. For Martin, a national alarm bulletin was issued on the morning of 27 December, but the forecast track remained imperfect.

After the storms and the Aude floods earlier that year, Météo-France developed a clearer way to explain weather dangers. Its first Vigilance map appeared on 1 October 2001. Departmental maps used four colours and informed the public, media and authorities simultaneously, with advice on how to act.

why_interesting.text: Strong contrasts between cold and warm air supported an exceptionally powerful Atlantic jet. Warm, moist air south of the storm tracks also supplied energy as water vapour condensed. This combination sustained rapid development close to Europe.

Lothar remained shallow while racing across the Atlantic, then deepened rapidly near the jet's exit. Published minimum-pressure estimates range from 960 to 962 hPa; Ulbrich and colleagues give 961 hPa at the French coast at 06 GMT 26 Dec. Its small size and fast movement produced abrupt pressure falls and rises.

Lothar left much of the large-scale Atlantic flow intact. Martin then developed through interaction with an upper-air disturbance and reached 965 hPa south of Brittany at 15 GMT 27 Dec in the same study. Unlike Lothar, it substantially changed the surrounding airflow.

During Lothar, DWD placed the strongest winds south of the centre, behind the occluded front. Mountain exposure increased some readings: DWD reports a measured gust of 259 km/h on Wendelstein at about 14 MEZ on 26 December, well above readings at lowland sites. It should not be treated as a representative wind across the affected area.

items.reanalysis: ERA5 represents two fast-moving lows: Lothar reaches about 969 hPa over Saarland at 10 UTC 26 Dec, and Martin about 964 hPa near southern Brittany at 17 UTC 27 Dec. Lothar is too shallow against the published surface analysis, while Martin's minimum pressure is much closer. Peak gusts at Orly, Chassiron and Wendelstein are below the reported measurements, especially at the exposed mountain site. The quarter-degree grid's smoothing of compact lows, coastlines and mountains is a likely contributor; modelled gusts also differ from the historical instantaneous measurements reported by Météo-France.

items.title: Hurricane Katrina

where.label: Gulf of Mexico, south-east Louisiana and coastal Mississippi

items.summary: Katrina rapidly strengthened over the Gulf of Mexico on 26-28 August 2005, reaching Category 5 with a central pressure of 902 hPa and maximum sustained winds of 150 knots. It weakened to Category 3 before landfalls near Buras, Louisiana, and the Louisiana-Mississippi border on 29 August, but its broad wind field drove a large storm surge onto the Mississippi coast. Surge and failures of levees and floodwalls flooded about 80% of New Orleans. The National Hurricane Center's revised US toll is 1,392 deaths, including direct, indirect and indeterminate causes, with total damage estimated at US$125 billion in 2005 dollars.

impacts.text: The National Hurricane Center's 2023 revision counts 1,392 deaths in the United States: 520 direct, 565 indirect and 307 with an indeterminate cause. These are whole-event figures, including deaths outside Louisiana and Mississippi. Earlier counts used different information: the 2006 NWS assessment provisionally listed 1,353 direct deaths, while early NHC reports put all deaths above 1,800.

Storm surge and waves destroyed homes, businesses and public buildings along the Mississippi coast. In New Orleans, overtopping and breaches of levees and floodwalls flooded about 80% of the city, with water reaching about 20 feet in places. Wind damaged buildings and power lines, and floods and destroyed bridges disrupted transport across the northern Gulf coast.

The updated National Hurricane Center report gives total US damage of US$125 billion in 2005 dollars, using NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information estimates. This is total damage, rather than insured loss alone. Flooded refineries, damaged offshore platforms and disrupted workplaces added to the storm's economic effects.

history.text: The NWS review found that NHC had forecast a major hurricane affecting the central Gulf coast, including New Orleans, about 56 hours before landfall. A hurricane watch covered south-east Louisiana from 10 a.m. CDT on 27 August; a warning followed that evening. At 10:11 a.m. CDT on 28 August, the New Orleans/Baton Rouge office issued its detailed bulletin on devastating damage and prolonged uninhabitable conditions. The review says broadcasters and emergency managers used its impact wording to prepare the public.

The post-event NWS assessment called for more resilient power and communications, stronger arrangements for offices backing each other up, and a separate code and standard wording for destructive hurricane wind warnings. These were recommendations following failures of infrastructure and confusion over warning formats during Katrina.

In 2017, NWS and NHC introduced separate operational storm surge watches and warnings for the continental US Gulf and Atlantic coasts. These distinguished the danger from rising coastal water from the wind hazard; the two can affect different places at different times.

why_interesting.text: Over the Gulf, a large anticyclone aloft gave Katrina weak wind shear and efficient outflow, allowing thunderstorms to organise around its centre. The ridge that had steered it west shifted towards Florida while a trough grew over the north-central United States. Katrina then curved north-west and north towards the Gulf coast.

Katrina underwent two periods of rapid intensification on 26-28 August. During the second, its central pressure fell by 32 hPa in the 12 hours ending at 12 UTC 28 Aug. Aircraft observations supported a minimum pressure of 902 hPa and an estimated maximum sustained surface wind of 150 knots at 18 UTC 28 Aug over the central Gulf.

Changes in the rings of thunderstorms around the eye helped Katrina weaken before landfall, while its wind field remained broad. NHC estimates sustained winds of 110 knots near Buras at 11:10 UTC 29 Aug and 105 knots at the Pearl River mouth at 14:45 UTC 29 Aug, both Category 3. Post-storm analysis reduced the Buras estimate from 120 to 110 knots because the winds aloft were not reaching the surface as efficiently as the usual adjustment assumed.

The weakening wind category did not remove the surge hazard. Katrina's broad onshore winds pushed water towards Mississippi, while waves generated during its stronger offshore phase raised water levels further. FEMA high-water-mark surveys put surge at about 24-28 feet along the coast around St Louis Bay, including a 27.8-foot mark at Pass Christian. This was a surveyed mark left by the water, rather than a continuously recorded peak.

Rising water in Lake Pontchartrain and the canals strained New Orleans' flood defences. Many breaches followed overtopping and erosion, but some floodwalls failed before water reached their tops. Heavy rain accompanied the hurricane, but the city's inundation cannot be explained as rainfall flooding alone.

The strongest gust at an official reporting station was 99 knots at Grand Isle C-MAN at 08:38 UTC 29 Aug; larger unofficial gusts were also reported. Rain was heaviest along and just west of the storm's track across south-east Louisiana and south-west Mississippi. The Slidell NWS office measured a storm total of 11.63 inches, about 295 mm.

items.reanalysis: ERA5 follows Katrina from the eastern Gulf on 27 August to south-east Louisiana on 29 August, but its minimum is 932 hPa south of Buras at 10 UTC 29 Aug, much later and less deep than the observed 902 hPa offshore at 18 UTC 28 Aug. At the observed peak hour it gives 952 hPa over the central Gulf, so the apparently closer landfall pressure does not mean it captures the earlier intensity; smoothing of the small eye and eyewall is a likely contributor. Grand Isle's maximum hourly gust is 48 m/s at 10 UTC 29 Aug, while New Orleans Lakefront's is 49 m/s at 13 UTC 29 Aug; the station instruments failed before the full wind event was sampled, and their brief gusts and differing exposure are not identical to an hourly model maximum. Slidell has 211 mm for the 48 hours ending 12 UTC 30 Aug against a measured storm total of about 295 mm, whose exact gauge reporting times are not stated, so the rain comparison is approximate; these atmospheric maps do not reconstruct storm surge, levee failure or flood depth.

items.title: Typhoon Hagibis

where.label: Izu Peninsula, Kanto and eastern Honshu

items.summary: Hagibis came ashore on Japan's Izu Peninsula just before 19:00 JST on 12 October 2019 and crossed Kanto. Moist air, a strengthening front and uplift over mountains produced exceptional rain well north of the centre. Hakone measured 922.5 mm on 12 October JST and 1,001.5 mm over 10–13 October. Floods, landslides and levee breaches caused widespread damage, with 105 deaths in Japan including 21 recognised deaths from indirect effects, calculated from FDMA's tables.

impacts.text: FDMA's tables dated 13 October 2020 imply 105 deaths in Japan, including 21 recognised deaths from indirect effects, with 3 people missing. This subtracts 13 deaths in separate rain from 25 October from its combined total of 118. The Cabinet Office's earlier Hagibis tally, dated 10 April 2020, was 91 deaths and 3 missing; the different dates and inclusion of later rain matter when comparing counts.

Rivers flooded across eastern Honshu, with 142 levee breaches. The Chikuma flooded Nagano, and the Abukuma flooded parts of Fukushima. Roads, bridges and railways were damaged, communities were cut off, and power and water supplies failed. At Hoyasu in Nagano, the Chikuma levee is estimated to have breached around 04:00 JST on 13 October.

The Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism's final estimate was about JPY 1.88 trillion in direct water-related damage from the 2019 event. This is a damage estimate, rather than an insured-loss total; the price year is not stated.

history.text: On 11 October, JMA warned of record rain at a press conference and invoked the 1958 Kano River Typhoon. Emergency heavy rain warnings began at 15:30 JST on 12 October and eventually covered Tokyo and 12 prefectures. The government review found that the historical comparison had not conveyed the urgency clearly enough.

Flooding continued downstream after emergency rain warnings ended. The government review set changes for the 2020 flood season: describe the change as a switch to a warning, provide information about continuing river rises, and continue public briefings. It also called for clearer explanations of which places faced the greatest danger.

why_interesting.text: Hagibis rapidly intensified over the western North Pacific. JMA's later best-track analysis placed its lowest central pressure at 915 hPa from 12 UTC 7 Oct to 06 UTC 10 Oct. It weakened while turning towards Japan, crossed the Izu Peninsula and Kanto, and became an extratropical cyclone at 03 UTC 13 Oct.

The large circulation carried warm, moist air towards Honshu. Cooler air spreading out from a continental high met that inflow, forming and strengthening a front north of the typhoon. Persistent rising air brought heavy rain before the central rain clouds arrived.

Mountain slopes added to the rain, especially where moist easterly and south-easterly winds climbed the terrain. JMA's experiments distinguished the causes: the front dominated in the Chikuma basin, while both the front and mountains contributed in the Abukuma basin and southern Kanto.

The rain was already concentrated north of the centre before the front became prominent. A later modelling study linked this earlier pattern to sloping upward motion between the typhoon and the westerly jet stream. As the storm approached the front, the main rain shifted towards its north-eastern side.

JMA reported more than 500 mm at 17 stations over 10–13 October. Hakone's 922.5 mm on 12 October set a national calendar-day rainfall record in JMA's station series. The total between local midnights differs from a rolling 24-hour total.

items.reanalysis: ERA5 follows Hagibis north towards Japan and across Kanto at 12 UTC 12 Oct, then out to sea. Its lowest central pressure is about 956 hPa at 06 UTC 10 Oct, south of Japan, compared with JMA's analysed 915 hPa. At Hakone, ERA5 gives about 310 mm from 12 UTC 10 Oct to 12 UTC 13 Oct, compared with the measured 1,001.5 mm during that interval; at Tokyo its strongest hourly gust is about 29 m/s at 08 UTC 12 Oct, compared with a measured 41.5 m/s at 21:14 JST. The broad track and rain episode are useful, but the coarse grid smooths the inner core, mountain uplift and local gusts; this is a likely explanation for the shortfalls.

items.title: Cyclone Amphan

where.label: Bay of Bengal, West Bengal and coastal Bangladesh

items.summary: Amphan rapidly intensified over the Bay of Bengal on 17–18 May 2020, reaching an estimated central pressure of 920 hPa in IMD's analysis. After weakening, it crossed the Sundarbans during 10-12 UTC 20 May with estimated sustained winds of 155–165 km/h, then passed close to Kolkata. Wind, coastal flooding and heavy rain damaged homes, crops, embankments and electricity supplies; Kolkata's Alipore observatory measured 240 mm in the 24 hours ending at 0830 IST on 21 May. IMD's report and its appended assessment give 98–99 deaths in West Bengal, while ECHO reported 26 deaths in Bangladesh on 25 May.

impacts.text: IMD's January 2021 report gives 98 deaths in West Bengal in its main text; the appended state assessment gives 99, so the reported range is 98–99. These are deaths attributed to the cyclone, including falling trees, electrocution, building collapse and other causes, rather than a separately defined direct-death count. ECHO's update of 25 May 2020 reported 26 deaths in Bangladesh without a direct/indirect breakdown.

The West Bengal assessment appended to IMD's report lists about 2.86 million houses damaged, alongside losses to farming, fisheries, embankments, roads, power and water supplies. Fallen trees blocked roads and delayed restoration. In Bangladesh, ECHO reported at least 220,000 houses damaged and about 500,000 families displaced as of 25 May.

West Bengal's sector assessment dated 6 June 2020, reproduced with IMD's report, estimated total damage and losses at INR 102,442 crore, about INR 1.02 trillion. This is an assessment across affected sectors, not an insured-loss figure; the basis in 2020 prices is not stated.

history.text: IMD's bulletin issued at 1645 IST on 16 May predicted rapid intensification. At 0845 IST on 17 May, it forecast a crossing between Sagar Island and Hatiya Islands on the afternoon or evening of 20 May, with the track pointing across the Sundarbans. An orange cyclone warning for West Bengal and north Odisha followed at 0845 IST on 18 May, and a red post-landfall outlook for inland districts at 2330 IST on 19 May.
During Amphan, IMD put the cyclone track on a geographical information system for the first time. It also sent notifications through the government's Umang mobile app and the Google network.

A subsequent study by Khan and colleagues demonstrated a practical system that combined tides, storm surge and waves. It recommended regular surveys of embankment heights and condition to improve local inundation forecasts; this was a research recommendation, rather than confirmation of a new operational service.

why_interesting.text: Warm water and a favourable atmosphere allowed the storm to strengthen quickly. IMD identified sea-surface temperatures of 30–31°C, a deep reservoir of ocean heat, little change in wind with height, and an increased supply of warm, moist air from across the equator.

IMD's best-track table raises the estimated sustained wind from 70 knots at 12 UTC 17 May to 130 knots at 18 UTC 18 May. The same table gives a lowest estimated central pressure of 920 hPa at 18 and 21 UTC 18 May over the west-central Bay. These are storm-intensity estimates over the sea, not station measurements.

Amphan first travelled north-northwest, then curved north-northeast towards the head of the Bay. IMD attributes this turn mainly to a broad clockwise circulation to its northeast in the middle and upper atmosphere, which steered it towards the Sundarbans.

The cyclone weakened before landfall as winds changed more strongly with height and the available ocean heat decreased farther north. It still crossed the Sundarbans during 10-12 UTC 20 May with IMD-estimated sustained winds of 155–165 km/h and gusts to 185 km/h, then carried damaging winds and heavy rain towards Kolkata.

Coastal flooding depended on more than wind speed. Wind and falling air pressure raised water levels, while tides and breaking waves altered the height and timing of the flood. Khan and colleagues found that embankment breaches were a major route for inland inundation in the Bangladesh locations they examined.

items.reanalysis: ERA5 follows Amphan north across the Bay and inland past Kolkata on 20 May, but its lowest central pressure is 941 hPa over the central Bay at 09 UTC 19 May, later and weaker than IMD's 920 hPa at 18 and 21 UTC 18 May. At Alipore it gives a peak gust of 29 m/s in the hour ending at 11 UTC 20 May, compared with IMD's reported 114 km/h maximum during 1600–2100 IST that day; at Khulna, ERA5's peak gust is 26 m/s in the hour ending at 18 UTC 20 May. ERA5 gives 73 mm at Alipore and 71 mm at Dum Dum for the 24 hours ending at 03 UTC 21 May, against 240 and 200 mm measured, while its 185 mm at Digha for the 48 hours ending then is close to the reported 180 mm. The likely reasons for the weaker core and lower Kolkata rainfall include smoothing of the compact cyclone and rain bands on the 0.25° grid, with local results also sensitive to the track.

items.title: Cyclone Gabrielle

where.label: North Island, especially Tairāwhiti and Hawke’s Bay

items.summary: Ex-tropical Cyclone Gabrielle brought destructive wind and rain to the North Island on 12–14 February 2023 NZDT, affecting Northland, Auckland and Coromandel first. It slowed near the Coromandel as an upper trough renewed its strength, feeding prolonged rain onto the hills of Tairāwhiti and Hawke’s Bay overnight on 13–14 February NZDT. Mokohinau measured a gust of 150 km/h on 12 February NZDT, while Napier Airport measured 175.8 mm of rain from 9am 13 February to 9am 14 February NZDT. NZHistory records 11 deaths in New Zealand; floods and slips damaged homes, farmland and transport links, and cut power and communications.

impacts.text: NZHistory counts 11 deaths in New Zealand from Gabrielle: eight in Hawke’s Bay, one at Te Karaka inland of Gisborne, and two volunteer firefighters caught in a landslide at Muriwai. Its account identifies deaths from the event rather than a formal direct-versus-indirect classification.

Floodwater reached homes in the Esk Valley and Te Karaka, while slips damaged houses on Auckland’s west coast. Roads were cut, communities lost power and communications, and floodwater and silt damaged orchards, vineyards and other farmland in Hawke’s Bay. A national state of emergency was declared on 14 February NZDT.

The Insurance Council of New Zealand’s February 2025 review puts Gabrielle’s insured losses at about NZ$1.8 billion, with the price basis not stated. This is insured loss alone; the larger Treasury damage range often quoted combines Gabrielle with the Auckland Anniversary floods.

history.text: MetService issued heavy-rain and strong-wind watches on 9 February NZDT, orange warnings on 11 February, and its first red warnings that afternoon. Agreement between forecast models increased its confidence in an impact on New Zealand.

The Government’s October 2024 response to the North Island severe-weather inquiry acknowledged gaps in public warnings. It reported a new arrangement with Radio New Zealand for broadcasts at set times in areas without power, and work with MetService to put civil-defence preparedness advice alongside severe-weather warnings.

why_interesting.text: Gabrielle arrived during a La Niña summer with unusually frequent easterly and north-easterly winds drawing warm, humid air towards New Zealand. Warm surrounding seas increased the moisture available to passing lows. Earlier rain had already left northern districts vulnerable to further flooding and slips.

Losing tropical status did not end the storm’s development. Interaction with the subtropical jet, temperature contrasts and an upper trough from the Tasman Sea renewed Gabrielle’s strength. The trough also slowed and turned the cyclone towards Great Barrier Island and the Coromandel late on 13 February NZDT.

The pause near the northern coast sustained moist winds against the steep hills behind Tairāwhiti and Hawke’s Bay. Uplift wrung rain from that air, and steep slopes carried water rapidly into rivers and low-lying settlements. This links the offshore track to the flooding overnight on 13–14 February NZDT.
The broad circulation spread strong winds across distant regions. Low pressure, onshore gales and swell raised coastal water levels, and storm surge hindered river drainage into the sea.

Napier Airport’s 175.8 mm from 9am 13 February to 9am 14 February NZDT was its wettest February day in records beginning in 1950. NIWA lists a 150 km/h gust measured at Mokohinau on 12 February NZDT. A later modelling study estimated that historical human-caused warming increased regional storm rainfall totals by about 10%.

items.reanalysis: ERA5 follows the slowdown near the Coromandel, reaching 967 hPa north-east of the peninsula at 15 UTC 13 Feb, before moving east towards East Cape on 14 February. At Napier Airport it gives 144 mm in the 24 hours ending 20 UTC 13 Feb, compared with 175.8 mm measured over the same period. Its peak Mokohinau gust is 31 m/s at 19 UTC 12 Feb, whereas NIWA reports 150 km/h on 12 February NZDT, so both strength and timing differ. The coarse grid smooths steep terrain and exposed sites; local rain and gust extremes, and the river flooding they produced, need finer detail than these weather maps provide.
